_about: Small talk: a line now and then about the café, the street, Paris and Nala's touches (how often: content/pacing.json).
when and weather are optional, as in welcome.json; about is only a note for you (Nala, café, street, Paris).
A line isn't used again until most of the others have been. Keep each to about 3 lines of 46 letters.

lines.text: Nala's handwriting is still on the chalkboard. Someone has drawn a little paw next to the prices.
The books on the bottom shelf are Nala's. Each book was picked out with thought.
The cushions in the cat bed were Nala's choice. Of course, the cats have already approved of them.
There's a note tucked into the menu: "Please don't feed the cats. They will lie to you."
None of the cups match. Nala likes it that way.
The chalkboard says "The cats are not on the menu." Underlined twice.
Someone has left a bookmark in one of Nala's books, halfway through.
The ivy on the bookcase is doing well. Someone waters it, though you never see who.
The radiator ticks quietly as it warms up.
There's a dent in the cushion of the cat bed, exactly cat-sized.
Your book now has a bookmark in it. You don't remember putting it there.
The lamp on the sideboard has a slightly crooked shade. Nobody has ever straightened it.
The marble of your table has a small chip in one corner. It's probably been there for years.
There are a few cream-coloured hairs on the chair across from you.
Somewhere behind you, a cup is set down on a saucer.
The candle on your table burns very slowly.
Down in the street, someone is pulling up the shutters of a bakery.
The first lights come on in the bakery down the street.
A delivery van stops below, then goes again.
Somewhere below, a scooter buzzes past and fades away.
It's the slow part of the afternoon. Nobody is in a hurry.
Someone across the street is watering the plants on their balcony.
The windows across the street light up, one by one.
A late bus goes by in the street below, almost empty.
Even the pigeons are asleep. Paris is very quiet at this hour.
A pigeon lands on the balcony rail, looks in, and leaves.
Paris has a lot of chimney pots. You try to count them, and give up.
If you wait for the hour, the Eiffel Tower sparkles.
On days like this, the whole city seems to have its windows open.
Grey sky, grey roofs. The lamps inside look warmer for it.
Umbrellas go by in the street below. Mostly black, one yellow.
Rain drums on the gutter outside the window.
Nobody is out in this. Except the pigeons, who look annoyed.
It's the kind of drizzle Paris is known for: not quite rain, never quite dry.
In the fog, the street below sounds closer than it is.
Snow muffles the street. Even the scooters sound polite.
